claims.claim: Google documents the Google Health API as the modern successor to the Fitbit Web API rather than a separate generic health-record product.
claims.evidence: The current landing page calls the Google Health API the Fitbit Web API evolved onto a more stable, consistent and scalable foundation.

claims.claim: An ordinary user can enable Google Health API in a Cloud project, create an OAuth client and authorize their own account as a test user.
claims.evidence: The setup guide provides direct Cloud project, API enablement, OAuth client, test-user and scope steps without requiring partner approval.

claims.claim: Google Health API projects are capped at 100 users while unverified, and supporting more than 100 users requires a third-party security review.
claims.evidence: The setup guide states that newly created OAuth clients have a 100-user cap in testing and production and that more than 100 users requires third-party security review.

claims.claim: OAuth refresh tokens issued while a project remains in Testing mode expire after seven days.
claims.evidence: The token behavior section states that Testing-mode refresh tokens are time-based and expire after seven days.

claims.claim: Google Health API requires user-consented scopes and provides read-only scopes for activity, health measurements, ECG, irregular-rhythm notifications, nutrition, profile, settings and sleep.
claims.evidence: The scope table lists these read-only collections and requires applications to handle partial consent.

claims.claim: The current Google Health API scope catalogue provides only write-only access for reproductive health, logged symptoms and mindfulness data.
claims.evidence: The available-scope table lists reproductive_health, logged_symptoms and mindfulness only with writeonly suffixes.

claims.claim: For supported data types, Google documents queries as far back as the data has been recorded with no API restriction on the total historical amount consumed.
claims.evidence: The historical-data section explicitly states that the API imposes no limitation on total history, while requiring pagination and bounded rollup windows.

claims.claim: The current Google Health API catalogue includes steps, energy, heart rate, HRV, sleep, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, temperature, ECG, irregular-rhythm notifications, VO2 max, exercise, nutrition, hydration and body measurements.
claims.evidence: Each family appears as a named data type with its record shape, available operations and OAuth scope.

claims.claim: Google Health API can distinguish Google/Fitbit wearable records from wider Google and reconciled third-party sources.
claims.evidence: Endpoint examples document google-wearables and google-sources data source families and include recording method, device and platform metadata.

claims.claim: Google Health API supports HTTPS webhook notifications for a documented subset of activity, exercise, sleep, heart, oxygen, respiratory, nutrition and body data.
claims.evidence: The webhook guide lists the supported data types and explains subscriber and user-subscription configuration.

claims.claim: No current Google Health API data type documents Fitbit Sleep Score, Daily Readiness, Stress Management Score, badges or coaching narratives as retrievable records.
claims.evidence: The page presents itself as the full data-type list and contains underlying sleep, activity and vital records, but no named record for these app-visible derived outputs.

claims.claim: Fitbit devices do not communicate directly with third-party applications; data becomes available after device synchronization through the Fitbit app.
claims.evidence: The third-party access section states that Fitbit devices sync exclusively with the Fitbit mobile app before third parties can access records through Google Health API.

claims.claim: Google provides a signed-in Google Health data export with examples including activity, exercise, sleep and heart rate, but the public help page does not provide an exhaustive versioned schema.
claims.evidence: The official page title and description offer a copy of Google Health data and name those categories; it does not publish a field-by-field archive contract.

claims.claim: Existing Fitbit Web API access and refresh tokens cannot be transferred to Google Health API, so users must re-consent.
claims.evidence: The migration guide describes different OAuth systems and explicitly says existing tokens cannot be transferred.

claims.claim: A legacy Fitbit Personal application can access the developer's own public and intraday data without submitting an intraday-access request.
claims.evidence: The application-types section says Personal applications are limited to the developer account and include intraday data without the request form.

claims.claim: Legacy Client and Server applications need case-by-case approval to retrieve other users' intraday data.
claims.evidence: The intraday guide says other-user access is granted case-by-case and only select applications receive it.

claims.claim: The legacy Fitbit Web API documents a limit of 150 requests per hour for each consenting user.
claims.evidence: The Rate Limits section gives 150 API requests per hour per user and documents the corresponding response headers.

claims.claim: The legacy activity-list response can include a TCX download link for an exercise.
claims.evidence: The endpoint schema includes activities.tcxLink and the example response supplies a Fitbit API TCX URL.
